subject: Culture
title: Naming and Lineage
description: A 60-second lesson on Naming and Lineage.

hook.text: Icelandic phone books are sorted by first name because surnames are just your father's name plus 'son' or 'dóttir.'

buildup.text: Patronymic systems tie your identity to your father's line. Matronymic ones trace the mother. Some cultures use both.

discovery.text: Surnames became mandatory in Europe only around the 1400s—tax collectors needed them to track people.

twist.text: In many African traditions your name tells the day you were born, the season, or the event marking your arrival.

climax.text: Changing your family name after immigration is a quiet act of cultural erasure that haunts later generations.

punchline.text: Your name is your family's first gift and story.

quiz.question: Why did surnames become mandatory in Europe?

details.summary: Names carry honor across generations. Patronymic systems (Johnson, ibn Saud) embed lineage into identity. Naming children after ancestors honors the dead. In some cultures, knowing and reciting one's genealogy stretching back centuries is a mark of honor and social standing.
details.whyItMatters: Naming traditions reveal how cultures transmit honor across generations. Your name literally carries the reputation of your ancestors and the expectations of your descendants.
takeaways: Patronymic naming links children's identities to fathers' reputations
Many cultures forbid naming children after living relatives
Reciting genealogy is a mark of status in Polynesian and Arab cultures

faq.question: Why do some cultures name children after ancestors?
faq.answer: Naming after ancestors honors the deceased, keeps their memory alive, and symbolically continues their presence in the family. In Jewish Ashkenazi tradition, children are named after deceased relatives only (never living ones).

faq.question: How do naming taboos work?
faq.answer: Many cultures restrict which names can be used. Chinese tradition avoids giving children names that contain characters from elders' names (bisui). Some Indigenous Australian cultures stop using a person's name after death.
